add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: implemented in commit `ed3d27e` ("Make xlint ignore frontmatter in agent definitions. Also don't check code blocks used as examples"), spec at `doc/plans/xlint-frontmatter-fence-skip.md`. Re-verified 2026-09-29 against the spec's own 12-point checklist — all pass, and the whole-repo run is still 0 violations.

- Frontmatter: `_frontmatter_exempt()` exempts line 1 through the closing `---`; an unclosed `---` falls back to linting the whole file; mid-file `---` is never treated as frontmatter.
- Fences: `_fence_exempt()` tracks opener char + length, never mixes ``` and ~~~, and carries an unclosed fence to EOF.
- Scope held: exemptions apply only to the `.md` branch of `check_file()` and only to the space-indent check; `.py` checks unchanged (confirmed a space-indented `.py` still fails).

**The indented-fence question in the comment above is answered by the spec, and the spec wins: an indented fence line stays a violation** ("house style forbids indented fences", spec line 60). So today's behaviour is correct-as-specified, not a bug. I confirmed this is what the code does and am filing the house-style change as its own ticket rather than fixing it here — that change reverses a documented rule and is the human's call.

add.issue.name: House style: should an indented code fence be a violation? (reverses the xlint spec)

edit.description.md:
Split out of `GBNEWPS`. That ticket's spec (`doc/plans/xlint-frontmatter-fence-skip.md`, line 60) says an indented fence line **stays a violation** — "house style forbids indented fences" — and the implementation matches that. A later comment on `GBNEWPS` argued the opposite and called it a bug.

Both are defensible; that is why it is a decision rather than a fix.

**The cost of the current rule.** A fence nested in a list item — the normal way to write one — can never be lint-clean. Verified 2026-09-29: a ```sh block indented under a `1. ` item has every one of its body lines flagged. Making such a file clean means editing inside a code block, which is worse than the violation. In `agent-notes-a4.md` the content was converted to tabs to dodge the check.

**Option A — keep the rule, fix the ergonomics.** Indented fences stay violations, but a *documented* opt-out (a marker, or exempting fences inside list items only) removes the trap without dropping the rule.

**Option B — exempt indented fences.** Test `line.lstrip()` for the fence characters instead of `line[0]`. One-line change in `_fence_exempt`, and indented code blocks become legal. Cost: house style genuinely loosens, and the 4-space-indented-code-block case loses its only signal — the spec's argument for keeping the rule is that markdown indented blocks *require* spaces, so the rule is the only thing flagging them.

Whichever wins, the fix is the same shape and wants a test with an indented fence whose body is space-indented — that case fails today.

`AGENTS.md` in this repo carries a large description of the XLib library structure and conventions that belongs in its own file, leaving AGENTS.md as rules rather than reference.

## Scope

Extract from `AGENTS.md` the library-structure material, currently clustered around lines 32-82:

- the library entry-point table (`<library>/SPEC.md`, dev-folder layout, entry point per library)
- the versioning scheme (`libraryname_major_minor_revision.py`) and the import rules — unversioned via `xlib_pins.py` vs explicit, and the rule that **libraries never use versionless imports, even in development**
- dev folders are not packages; no `__init__.py` at the library root, but internal subfolders may have one
- `VERSIONS.md` per versioned library, newest first
- the entry-file rule: `<libraryname>.py` holds only the public interface, internals in separate files (e.g. `csv_tok.py`)
- the bundler's name-prefixing behaviour (`tokenize` in `csv_tok.py` → `csv_tok_tokenize`) and its consequences, including how relative imports between a library's own modules are handled

## The move

Create a dedicated reference doc (candidate: `doc/library-structure.md`) and replace the extracted section in `AGENTS.md` with a pointer to it. Keep the *rules* that an agent must follow on every edit where they are seen; move the *explanatory and structural* material out. The line between the two is the judgement call in this ticket and needs deciding deliberately, section by section — several items above are both (e.g. "never use versionless imports" is a rule; the naming scheme it references is reference).

## Why

- AGENTS.md is a rules file, read on every session. Structural reference is bulk that is only needed when working on library code.
- The current file mixes "what to do" with "how the library is shaped", which is what makes it hard to keep short — and shrinking it is the goal of 28Y59JV ("Slim AGENTS.md — give every remaining rule an explicit home"). This is the largest single extraction that work has available; do them in sequence, not in parallel, so the two don't fight over the same lines.

## Notes

- Related: 28Y59JV. Sequence after or as part of it, and keep them from overlapping on the same text.
- No absolute machine paths in the new file (see 7HP67R2); the same constraint as any tracked file.
- The new file is reference, not a state document — no `plans/` lifecycle applies.
